newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Bradford & Bingley cites mutual benefits.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bradford & Bingley cites mutual benefits.

text.p: Britain's Bradford & Bingley Building Society said on Wednesday its policy of remaining mutually owned rather than converting to Plc bank status had brought benefits in terms of asset growth and it expected this to continue.

"In 1996 our asset growth was 50 percent above our natural market share and we expect that to continue -- it will be very hard for the soon-to-be banks to compete," finance director John Smith told Reuters.
Rather than converting, as rival home loan and savings organisations such as the Halifax and the Woolwich plan this year, Bradford & Bingley is commited to remaining a mutual.

Bradford & Bingley distributes part of its profits to members though lower mortgage rates and higher savings rates and said it was doubling the scale of this process to two million stg per week this year, or 100 million stg on an annual basis.

Smith said this had resulted in mortgage rates 1/4 point below its rivals. Savings rates are harder to compare given the wide range of products, but Smith said its rates in general were better than those of the societies planning to convert.
Smith denied that converting societies might be able to attract higher quality new business -- for example from people to whom they would be able to sell other products.
"The most discerning customers will seek the best rates, so that should help the quality of the business," Smith said.
Bradford & Bingley earlier reported a fall in profits after tax to 56.6 million stg in 1996 from 107.7 million in 1995, reflecting the new policy of offering members benefits.

Operating profits were also affected by a 15 million stg charge for the society's reorganisation and redundancy programme and a 20 million stg reduction in pre-tax profit as a result of a more conservative accounting policy which takes into account the impact of mortgage incentives such as discounts and cashbacks.

The society's management expenses fell to 1.16 percent of mean assets from 1.19 percent, excluding the exceptional items, and it said it planned further reductions. Bad and doubtful debts dropped by 86 percent to 1.8 million stg, and the number of borrowers more than twelve months in arrears fell by 37 percent.

Smith echoed other industry comments on the UK housing market, saying it was showing signs of recovery but that this was not uniform, with London and south east England boosted by special factors such as an influx of people from Hong Kong.
"We think it (the market) will recover in 1997, but not boom away as it did in the '80s, which none of us want to see," he said.
